overview.text: Goryeo ruled the Korean peninsula from 918 to 1392, between the Unified Silla and Joseon periods. Its court supported Buddhism, and artists made refined celadon ceramics with green glazes and distinctive inlaid decoration. The dynasty also sponsored the Tripitaka Koreana, a Buddhist canon carved on more than 80,000 woodblocks. Mongol invasions in the thirteenth century forced the court to retreat to Ganghwa Island; later, Goryeo maintained close ties with the Mongol-led Yuan dynasty, including marriages between royal families. Political divisions over relations with the rising Ming dynasty helped bring Goryeo to an end, after which Yi Seonggye founded Joseon.

overview.text: The Corinthian War was a struggle in ancient Greece from 395 to 387/386 BCE. Athens, Corinth, Argos, and Boeotia opposed Sparta after Sparta’s victory in the Peloponnesian War had made its power and interference alarming to former allies. Fighting took place on land and at sea; a naval defeat near Cnidus in 394 weakened Spartan control in the Aegean. Persia influenced the conflict by supplying resources and later backing Sparta. The King’s Peace, arranged with Persian involvement, ended the war and recognized Persian control of Greek cities in Asia Minor. Sparta remained influential in mainland Greece, but its dominance faced continuing resistance.

overview.text: German peasants were rural farmers and villagers living under varied lords and obligations in the Holy Roman Empire. In 1524–1525, many joined a widespread revolt now called the German Peasants’ War. Their complaints centered on serfdom, rents, labor services, access to communal land, and control of local churches. The Twelve Articles, drafted in Memmingen in 1525, expressed demands such as choosing pastors, reducing unfair dues, and ending serfdom; their writers justified these requests with Christian scripture. The revolt was defeated and repression followed. Historians still debate exactly how the uprising related to the Protestant Reformation, so its economic and local political demands deserve attention in their own right.

overview.text: William the Conqueror was duke of Normandy before becoming king of England in 1066. After landing in southern England, he defeated King Harold Godwinson’s army at the Battle of Hastings on 14 October and was crowned at Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day. Winning the battle did not immediately secure the kingdom: William faced revolts and used castles and military campaigns to strengthen Norman rule. His government ordered a detailed survey of English landholding that produced the Domesday Book in 1086. The conquest changed who held land and power in England, and the castles associated with Norman rule became a lasting feature of its landscape.

overview.text: The Battle of Pharsalus in 48 BCE was the decisive clash between Julius Caesar and Pompey during a Roman civil war. It took place in Thessaly, in central Greece, after both commanders maneuvered for an advantage. Pompey had the larger cavalry force, but Caesar held infantry in reserve to meet an attack on his flank. The reserve helped turn back Pompey’s cavalry, leaving his army exposed; Pompey fled after his forces broke. He was killed soon afterward in Egypt. Caesar’s victory greatly strengthened his position, although opposition to him continued elsewhere. The battle illustrates how a civil war could make Roman armies fight one another for control of the republic.

overview.text: Pedro was the regnal name of Brazil’s first two emperors, father and son. Pedro I declared independence from Portugal in 1822 and became the new empire’s first ruler. He issued the Constitution of 1824, then abdicated in 1831 in favor of his young son, Pedro II. A regency governed until Pedro II took power; his reign lasted until the monarchy ended in 1889. Their shared name makes it important to distinguish the two rulers and their eras. During Pedro II’s reign, his daughter Princess Isabel signed the 1888 Golden Law as regent, legally abolishing slavery; the law itself identifies her as the person who sanctioned it.

overview.text: Uyghurs are a Turkic people with a long history in Central Asia and a major presence in the Xinjiang region of China. A Uyghur steppe empire flourished in the eighth and ninth centuries, but its rule ended in 840. Groups then established communities farther west, including a kingdom in the Tarim Basin where Buddhist temples and cave art became important. Religious practices changed over time: earlier Uyghur communities included Buddhists, while Islam later became the dominant faith for most Uyghurs. Xinjiang lay on Silk Road routes that connected peoples across Eurasia. Uyghur cultural traditions include Muqam, a performance practice recognized by UNESCO.

overview.text: The Great Stand on the Ugra River was a 1480 confrontation between the forces of Ivan III of Moscow and Akhmat Khan of the Great Horde. The armies faced one another along the Ugra, a tributary of the Oka, after Moscow’s tribute payments to the Horde had dwindled and stopped. Akhmat waited for help from the Polish-Lithuanian side, but his army eventually withdrew without a decisive pitched battle. The episode is often treated as a marker of Moscow’s escape from Horde overlordship. That interpretation should not suggest the wider Tatar political world vanished in 1480: the Great Horde and other khanates continued to shape regional affairs afterward.

overview.text: Five Eyes is an intelligence-sharing partnership among Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Its roots lie in British-American cooperation on communications intelligence during World War II. A formal U.S.–U.K. agreement signed in 1946 established a framework for sharing sensitive signals intelligence; Canada, Australia, and New Zealand later became partners. The arrangement concerns information such as intercepted communications, codebreaking, translation, and analysis. It is more than a name for five countries: it describes longstanding cooperation among their intelligence agencies. The partnership has also provided a basis for broader coordination on security problems, although each country remains responsible for its own policies.

overview.text: The Three Kingdoms period followed the collapse of China’s Han dynasty in 220 CE. Instead of one ruling house, three rival states—Wei, Shu Han, and Wu—contested power. The era is conventionally dated from 220 to 280, when the Jin dynasty completed a short-lived reunification. Political fragmentation continued in later centuries, so this reunion did not begin a long, stable empire. The period became especially famous through the much later novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms, which turned historical figures and conflicts into enduring stories. Its literary fame should be distinguished from the surviving historical record, which shows a complex era of shifting rulers and warfare.
